top_cited_works.title: Piezoelectric-Based Vibration Reduction of Turbomachinery Bladed Disks via Resonance Frequency Detuning
top_cited_works.abstract: Piezoelectric-based resonance frequency detuning can alleviate unwanted vibration of turbomachinery blades, thus reducing the dangers of high-cycle fatigue while also decreasing the blade weight. This semiactive approach applies to structures that are subjected to frequency-sweep excitation and involves altering the structural stiffness (here, by switching the piezoelectric electrical boundary conditions) to avoid a resonant condition, thus limiting the blade response. Detuning requires two switches per resonance/excitation frequency crossing, including a switch back to the original the original state,many fewer than other semiactive approaches that require four switches per cycle of vibration.Resonance frequencydetuningapplies to anymode of vibrationwith apositive electromechanical coupling coefficient, and it provides the greatest normalized vibration reduction for slow sweeps, low damping, and high coupling coefficient. top_cited_works.title: Damping Models for Shear Beams with Applications to Spacecraft Wiring Harnesses
top_cited_works.abstract: Spacecraft wiring harnesses can fundamentally alter a spacecraft’s structural dynamics, necessitating a model to predict the coupled dynamic response of the structure and attached cabling. Although a beam model including first-order transverse shear can accurately predict vibration resonance frequencies, current time domain damping models are inadequate. For example, common proportional damping models result modal damping that depends unrealistically on the frequency. Inspired by a geometric rotation-based viscous damping model that provides frequency independent modal damping in an Euler–Bernoulli formulation, a viscous damping model with terms associated with the shear and bending angles is presented. The model provides modal damping that is approximately constant in the bending-dominated regime (low mode numbers), increasing by at most 6% for a particular selection of bending and shear angle-based damping coefficients. In the shear-dominated regime (high mode numbers), damping values increase linearly with mode number and in proportion to the shear angle-based damping coefficient. top_cited_works.title: Uterine blood flow and uterine renin secretion
top_cited_works.abstract: Experiments were carried out in pregnant nephrectomized rabbits to determine the relationship between uterine blood flow and uterine renin secretion. Uterine blood flow was measured by the percentage distribution of radioactive microspheres injected into the left ventricle which lodged in uterus and placenta, and cardiac output was measured by dye dilution. In 40 animals, 24 hr after nephrectomy, uterine blood flow was 4.7+/-0.4% of cardiac output and absolute flow 32.4+/-3 ml/100 g per min. Plasma renin activity (PRA) in uterine vein, 994+/-182 ng/100 ml per hr, was higher than in carotid artery, 832+/-143 (P < 0.025). With reduction of uterine blood flow from 4.7+/-0.5 to 1.95+/-0.3% of cardiac output and absolute flow from 30.8+/-4.6 to 8.8+/-2 ml/100 g per min, uterine vein PRA rose from 1434+/-234 to 4430+/-300 (P < 0.001), and carotid artery PRA from 1009+/-200 to 2300+/-350 (P < 0.01). Hemorrhagic hypotension caused uterine vein PRA to increase from 913+/-293 to 3638+/-1276 (P < 0.001) and carotid artery PRA from 774+/-252 to 1730+/-433 (P < 0.01). recent_works.title: Development of Baseline Mathematical Hydrodynamics Models for Submersibles with Adaptive Hydrofoils
recent_works.abstract: Maneuverability and endurance are two key design considerations for diesel-electric submersibles. Exterior hull modifications were considered for opportunities to improve mobility, limiting the impact on the interior layout and design of the submarine. Morphing structures have been tested on aerospace applications and preceding research analyzed hydrodynamic modeling methods of adaptive fins on submersibles. Previous research analyses indicated that rapidly-computed potential flow-based hydrodynamic coefficients could be fused with higher fidelity computational fluid dynamics analyses to generate a model that could predict the loads experienced by a submersible with adapting hydrofoils. With the potential flow theory coefficients derived in previous research to account for adapting hydrofoil effects, a comprehensive high-fidelity baseline hydrodynamic model needed to be built. This paper covers the setup, simulation, design, and output of the high-fidelity CFD-based hydrodynamic model of the baseline submersible. recent_works.title: Experimental Analysis of a Novel Piezoelectric Flow Injection Valve for Flutter Boundary Mapping in Turbomachinery
recent_works.abstract: Flutter remains a challenge for turbomachinery design and operation. Current testing methods often rely on a binary “flutter” / “no flutter” determination to identify the flutter boundary. Measuring actual aeromechanical damping provides a more accurate determination of the flutter boundary and reduces risk of entering flutter. Moreover, it provides data validation for engine simulations. It is possible to measure aeromechanical damping by using actuators to excite modes of interest during engine testing and measuring their vibratory response. However, the limited bandwidth and authority of current actuators restrict how broadly this approach can be applied. Our collaborative team recently developed a flow-injection valve using piezoelectric actuation to expand testing. This paper presents the development of a novel Non-contact Oscillatory Valve Actuator, NOVA, and characterizes its performance in benchtop testing. Primary performance metrics include mass flow rate variation through the valve (authority) and frequency of operation (bandwidth). recent_works.title: Damping Modulation of Dampened Kapton Surfaces
recent_works.abstract: Vibrating droplets exhibit complex sloshing motion, an understudied behavior in drop physics. In general, sloshing involves a combination of droplet motion, deformation, and mass redistribution in all three dimensions. For microflyers in damp or wet environments, the dynamics of these drops on flight surfaces can significantly alter performance. As part of a larger project studying droplet adhesion and ejection on flexible, millimeter-scale wings, the current effort addresses the influence of a sloshing droplet on a highly flexible structural element inspired by insect wings. The ability of drops to deform and even relocate complicates the task of determining the dynamics of a microflyer wing. Our current understanding of sloshing stems from previous work on droplets of various viscosities placed at the end on the top surface of a cantilever beam. These experiments were repeated across a range of various beam thicknesses and demonstrated an influence that depended on the beam’s excitation frequency. recent_works.title: A piezoelectric-based, high-frequency flow valve for non-contact excitation of turbomachinery for flutter boundary mapping
recent_works.abstract: A key indicator of flutter risk in turbomachinery is aeromechanical damping, which decreases when approaching a flutter boundary. Current flutter testing methods require flutter boundary crossing and only provide binary flutter/no flutter data. Aeromechanical Identification Methodology (AIM) allows damping measurements to be collected during operation. These measurements allow identification of flutter boundaries without requiring the test article to encounter flutter. This approach is safer and enables AIM operation over a wider range of conditions. This approach would significantly improve present flutter testing; however, current available actuators’ low-frequency capabilities have limited AIM’s applicability to commercial fans. AIM utilizes noncontact actuation, avoiding concerns associated with on-blade actuation, such as added structural mass or wiring through a slip ring. A proposed piezoelectric-based, high-frequency flow valve presents a non-contact actuation method by injecting oscillatory flow during engine testing, offering a solution to the previously limited data range. recent_works.title: Development of Hydrodynamics Models With Adaptive Hydrofoil Approximations for Submersible Simulations and Control
recent_works.abstract: One challenge of traditional miniature submarine design is mobility, which includes both maneuverability and endurance. They typically are powered by diesel-electric systems with batteries that substantially increase the submarines' average density. Consequently, the number of batteries must be limited, and their density is typically offset with foam or entrapped air. Miniature submarines are densely packed with components and have relatively small hydroplanes in comparison to their hull size, both of which limit maneuverability. Morphing structures have been proposed and applied for aircraft; this research applies the ideas to non-fixed hydroplane submersible systems with the objective of increasing maneuverability and maximum range. Adapting hydroplanes would alter submarine dynamics and control, so creating a hydrodynamic loading model that can account for adapting hydrofoils is critical.
